finding: France mobile outgoing voice per customer per month, Q1 2011 (before Free Mobile, Jan 2012)
citation: ARCEP Observatoire des marches T1 2011, table 'Trafic mensuel moyen voix sortant'
notes: Flat at about 2h13-2h20 through 2010.

finding: France mobile voice per customer per month, Q1 2013, after unlimited plans spread
notes: ARCEP credits traffic to other networks (+35.4% y/y) to 'la generalisation des offres illimitees'. Use rose about 27% vs Q1 2011, so unlimited raised use (against), but by a bounded amount.

finding: France mobile voice per customer per month, Q1 2015
notes: A plateau 3 years after unlimited became standard: +36% vs 2011, then flat. This is satiation.

finding: France mobile voice per mobile-device holder per month, 2023
notes: Basis differs (device holders vs customers). About 0.5% of waking time: nobody 'calls 24 h a day'. Use settled at a ceiling about 1.5x pre-unlimited.

finding: France mobile data per smartphone customer per month, Q1 2013
France mobile data per customer per month, Q1 2015
France mobile data per user per month, 2023
value: 14 GB; +about 2 GB every year since 2018; total traffic +20% in 2023
notes: About 26x the 2015 level. No satiation for data (a 'good' whose content keeps expanding: video).

finding: Unlimited vs very large capped plans, data use
value: +20% in high-GDP countries; -40 to -45% in low-GDP countries; total (mobile+Wi-Fi) varies only about 2.5x across plans
citation: Ericsson Mobility Report article 'Shifting mobile data consumption with data plans' (2017)
notes: Unlimited raises mobile data use modestly where incomes are high. Mostly substitution from Wi-Fi.

finding: Flat-rate bias: share of consumers choosing a flat rate that costs more than pay-per-use
value: up to 46.4% (criterion 1); up to 29.3% (criterion 2); pay-per-use bias <=5.8%
notes: Many flat-rate (internet) subscribers use LESS than the break-even volume. Flat rate does not induce maximal use. Insurance effect = people pay for security.

finding: Household food waste differs little across country income groups (2022)
value: about 7 kg/capita/yr difference between HIC, UMC and LMC averages; households 631 Mt of 1.05 bn t total
citation: UNEP Food Waste Index Report 2024 (via UN News)
notes: Richer, more food-secure countries do NOT waste less. Security alone does not cut waste. Rural households in middle-income countries waste less (feed and compost use).

finding: Global per-capita waste similar across income groups (2019)
value: 74 kg/capita/yr, 'remarkably similar from lower-middle income to high-income'
citation: UNEP Food Waste Index Report 2021 (UNCCD library page)
notes: The 79/76/91 kg values by income group could NOT be verified and are not used.

finding: Food waste follows an inverted U with income: rises at middle incomes as people 'overbuy ... to avoid running out', then stabilises and declines
citation: Lopez Barrera, Vieira & Ferreira, Am. J. Agric. Econ., doi:10.1002/ajae.70040 (press release Texas A&M 2026-04-30)
notes: Precautionary overbuying is a named mechanism (supports the idea that secure access cuts one waste channel). But waste rises from the poor to the middle (against the claim that security cuts waste). Verified from a press release only.

finding: UK self-reported household food waste during COVID lockdown (Apr 2020) vs a year earlier
citation: WRAP, Citizens and food during lockdown (May 2020)
notes: Waste fell when access felt LESS secure (careful use and planning). Self-reported. Leeds summary says it rebounded after lockdown (+31%, not verified).

finding: Ireland grocery sales, week to 15 Mar 2020 (panic buying)
value: +23% y/y; +16% w/w; toilet roll +181%; pasta +199%; rice +123%; hand sanitiser +2,412%
notes: A scarcity scare causes large, short stockpiling spikes concentrated in storable essentials. Credible guaranteed supply plus fixed prices should damp this.

finding: Scarcity shifts attention and causes over-borrowing (experiments)
notes: Mechanism support only. No consumption-volume number.

finding: Food insecurity and high body weight: positive association in 125-study meta-analysis, restricted to adult women in high-income countries
citation: Nettle, Andrews & Bateson 2017, Behav. Brain Sci. 40:e105
notes: Insurance hypothesis: insecurity drives fat storage and over-eating. Supports the hypothesis for one subgroup only (women, HIC). Not found in men or in LMICs.

finding: India: per-capita calorie intake fell while real incomes rose
value: rural 2,240 kcal (1983) to 2,047 kcal (2004-05), -8.6% (from search snippet)
notes: The fetched abstract confirms only that intake is 'declining' despite rising incomes. The kcal numbers were not seen in fetched text. Shows calorie satiation and low calorie-income elasticity, partly from less physical work.

finding: Ad libitum ultra-processed vs unprocessed diet (inpatient RCT, n=20)
value: +508 kcal/day; +0.9 kg vs -0.9 kg in 2 weeks
notes: Over-eating under secure, unlimited access depends on food FORM. Security does not cure it. Robust replacement for the retracted Wansink buffet studies (not used).

finding: Kenya GiveDirectly UCT: consumption, food security, temptation goods
value: consumption +USD 35.66/month (+23%) from J-PAL summary; no increase in alcohol/tobacco
notes: The fetched abstract confirms a 'strong consumption response' and that monthly transfers improve food security more than lump sums. The +23% figure and 'no temptation increase' were search-only. Lump sums went to durables (savings constraint).

finding: Cash transfers and temptation goods: 44 estimates from 19 studies, almost all null or negative
citation: Evans & Popova 2017, Econ. Dev. Cult. Change 65(2):189-221
notes: The 44/19 count and 'no significant impact or a significant negative impact' were verified. The -0.18 SD was NOT verified.

finding: Direct rebound for household energy services (OECD)
notes: Cheaper energy services raise use, but by less than the saving. The 10% lower bound and per-service values were not verified.

finding: Road transport direct rebound meta-analysis
notes: Not verified.

finding: Individual metering and billing on actual consumption vs flat-rate (per m2) billing
citation: HM Government of Gibraltar guidance on EED Art. 9(3), 2018 (citing EU studies)
notes: Flat-rate (unmetered) heat leads to more use: a counter-case to the phone analogy. Other figures (15-20% single building; about 20% older buildings EC; 11% Italy) are search-only.

finding: Tallinn fare-free PT (2013): PT usage after almost 1 year
citation: Cats, Susilo & Reimal 2017, Transportation (abstract via World Transit Research)
notes: Snippets (not verified) say car use fell only about 5%, car trip length rose, and walking trips fell. Induced demand, little car substitution.

finding: Dunkirk fare-free buses (2018): ridership
notes: Zero price produced large induced use. Car-switch figures (48% of riders use the bus 'instead of car' at times; 20% of new riders ex-drivers) are search-only.

finding: Luxembourg: car commuting share 2011 vs 2021 despite free PT (from Mar 2020)
notes: Free transit did not shift mode much. Supply and convenience dominate price.

finding: Finland basic income 2017-18, Mincome (Dauphin 1974-79): consumption composition
notes: Searched briefly: these trials report employment, well-being and health, not consumption volumes or stockpiling. No number used.
